title: User Interface
summary: Build Lightning Web Components that react, talk, call Apex and stay secure, and still handle Aura and Visualforce when the exam asks.

lessons.title: Reactivity: what makes LWC re-render
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, develop Lightning Web Components using reactive properties, decorators and template directives

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A component shows data on screen. When that data changes, the screen should redraw by itself. That redraw is a **re-render**. **Reactivity** is the rule for which changes LWC notices. Get it wrong and your code runs, but the screen still shows the old value.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Picture a scoreboard that only watches **which sign hangs on the hook**. Hang a new sign and the board updates. Scribble on the old sign and nobody notices. Where it stops: `@track` makes LWC watch the scribbles too, but only on plain objects and arrays.

cards.title: Every field is reactive
cards.body: Since Spring '20, **every class field** is reactive. If the template uses a field and you **reassign** it, the component re-renders. No decorator needed: `count = 0;` then `this.count++` just works. Changing a property *inside* an object or array is a **mutation**. LWC misses that by default.

cards.title: The 3 decorators (tags that give a field powers)
items: `@api`: makes a property or method public, so the parent, App Builder or Flow can set it
`@track`: deep watching, so changes *inside* a plain object or array re-render
`@wire`: data streamed in by a wire adapter (a ready-made data feed)

cards.title: Mutation vs reassignment
cards.body: Editing inside the object is missed. Handing over a new object is seen (or add `@track`).

cards.title: No math in templates
cards.body: Templates allow only plain names like `{fullName}`, never `{first + last}`. Put the logic in a **getter** (a function you read like a field): `get fullName() { return this.first + ' ' + this.last; }`. A getter runs again on every render, so it always shows fresh values.

cards.title: Small rules the exam loves
items: Every `for:each` or `iterator` item needs a `key`: a unique string or number from the data, **never the index**
Conditions: `lwc:if`, `lwc:elseif`, `lwc:else`
A Boolean `@api` property should **default to false**. Writing the attribute in markup means true
`Set`, `Map`, `Date` and class instances are **not** watched, even with `@track`. Assign a new one

cards.body: `@api` **objects are read-only to the child.** Writing `this.record.Name = 'x'` in the child throws an error, because the parent owns that data. Clone it into a private field, or fire an event so the **owner** changes it. Adding `@track` next to `@api` is not allowed and doesn't help.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"New box, new look."** Hand LWC a new value and it redraws. Change what's inside the old box and it only notices with `@track`, and only for plain objects and arrays.

terms.say: When the screen redraws a component to show new data. LWC does it by itself when a value it watches changes.
The rule for which changes LWC notices. If it notices a change, it redraws the screen. If it misses one, the old value stays.
Changing something inside an object or array, like editing one line of a list. LWC misses it unless the field has @track. A whole new object is always seen.
A tag that makes LWC watch inside a plain object or array too. Then changing one piece redraws the screen. It doesn't watch Set, Map or Date.
Makes a property or method public. Then the parent, App Builder or Flow can set it. The child must not change an @api object itself.
Fills a field with data from a wire adapter, a ready-made data feed. When its inputs change, fresh data streams in by itself.
A function you read like a field, like fullName. It runs again on every render, so it always shows fresh values. Use it instead of math in templates.
A unique label for each item in a list loop, taken from the data, like a record Id. LWC uses it to tell items apart. Never use the index.
Shows a part of the template only when a value is true. Add lwc:elseif and lwc:else for the other cases.

lessons.title: Lightning Data Service & the wire service
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use Lightning Data Service, wire adapters and base record components to work with Salesforce data

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Most components just read or save one record. **Lightning Data Service (LDS)** does that for you, with no Apex. It also checks the user's permissions for you: **CRUD, FLS and sharing**. That means: may they use this object, see this field, and see this record?

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: LDS is a **shared whiteboard** in a classroom. Every component reads the same board. When one writes a new value, everyone sees it at once. Where it stops: Apex writes on its own paper. LDS doesn't see those changes until you tell it.

cards.title: One shared cache
cards.body: LDS reads and writes through the **UI API**. It **caches** records (keeps a copy in the browser) and **shares** that copy. So when one LDS component saves a record, every other LDS component showing it updates. To save in code, use `createRecord`, `updateRecord` or `deleteRecord` from `lightning/uiRecordApi`. Each handles one record per call.

cards.title: `getRecord` + `getFieldValue`
cards.body: Reads the Account Name; `'$recordId'` makes it fetch again whenever `recordId` changes.

In `getRecord`, one field in `fields` that the user can't see makes the whole call fail. Even the fields they *can* see disappear. Put fields some users may not see in `optionalFields`. Those are quietly left out instead.

cards.title: Pick a base record component (ready-made forms)
items: `lightning-record-form`: fastest, least code. Modes `view`, `edit` and `readonly`, but little layout control
`lightning-record-view-form` + `lightning-output-field`: read-only, your own layout
`lightning-record-edit-form` + `lightning-input-field`: your own layout, plus `onsubmit` and `onsuccess` hooks. Add `lightning-messages` to show save errors

cards.title: Change values before saving
cards.body: In the edit form's `onsubmit`, stop the save, set `Status__c`, then submit the changed fields yourself.

cards.title: Free extras
items: Import fields from `@salesforce/schema/...`, not strings. Salesforce then **checks the field exists** and **blocks deleting it** while you use it
Base components come with ARIA, keyboard support and labels. Always set `label` (`variant="label-hidden"` hides it) and give icons `alternative-text`

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"One whiteboard, everyone in sync, permissions checked."** A field some users can't see goes in the *optional* row.

terms.say: Salesforce's built-in helper that reads and saves records for components, with no Apex. It keeps one shared copy and checks the user's permissions.
Four things you can do to records: Create, Read, Update, Delete. CRUD says which of the four a user may do on an object, like Account.
Field-level security. Rules for single boxes on a record. A user may see a name, but the Salary box can be hidden or locked.
The Salesforce service LDS uses to read and save records. It follows the user's permissions, so users only get what they may see.
A copy kept in the browser so it needn't ask the server again. LDS shares one copy, so every component shows the same record.
A ready-made way to read one record's fields through LDS. If the user can't see one field in fields, the whole call fails.
Fields for getRecord that some users may not see. A field the user can't see is quietly left out, and the rest still loads.
The quickest ready-made form for one record. It can view or edit with very little code, but you can't control the layout much.
A ready-made edit form where you place each field yourself. Its onsubmit lets you change values before saving, and onsuccess runs after.
Importing a field by reference instead of typing its name as text. Salesforce checks the field exists and blocks deleting it while you use it.

lessons.title: Calling Apex & keeping data fresh
lessons.objective: Given a set of requirements, develop Lightning Web Components that call Apex methods using wire or imperative calls

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes LDS isn't enough. You need a custom query or logic, so you call **Apex** (Salesforce's server code). There are two ways. **Wire** it, and data flows in by itself. Or call it **imperatively**: you call it yourself, like a normal function, when you need it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Wiring is a **newspaper subscription**. It arrives by itself and comes again when your address changes. An imperative call is **phoning a shop** when you decide to. Where it stops: the newspaper is read-only. Saving data always means phoning.

cards.title: Apex method checklist
items: `static`
`public` or `global`
`@AuraEnabled` (lets components call it)
Import it: `import getX from '@salesforce/apex/MyCtrl.getX';`

cards.title: `@wire` needs `cacheable=true`
cards.body: To `@wire` a method, mark it `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`. **Cacheable** means the browser may reuse the answer, so the method must be **read-only**. Any DML (a database save) inside it fails at runtime. To save data, call a non-cacheable method **imperatively**. It returns a Promise (an answer that arrives later).

cards.title: Wire with `refreshApex`
cards.body: Keeps the whole wired result, then hands that exact object to `refreshApex` after saving.

cards.title: Apex changed an LDS record?
cards.body: LDS can't see what Apex changed. After the Apex call finishes, call `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable([{ recordId }])` from `lightning/uiRecordApi`. LDS fetches the record again and updates every component showing it. It replaces the older `getRecordNotifyChange`. Or skip Apex: `updateRecord` updates the LDS cache by itself.

cards.title: Wire gotchas
items: `'$recordId'` with the `$` passes the live value. Without it, you send the word `'recordId'`
If a parameter is `undefined`, the wire waits and calls nothing
Wired data is **read-only**. Copy it before you change it
Only `@AuraEnabled` properties of an Apex class reach the browser
A cacheable method called imperatively can still return the cached answer

cards.body: Classic wrong answer: pass `result.data` to `refreshApex`. That does nothing. `refreshApex` needs the whole provisioned value, the object that holds data and error. Another wrong answer: mark a saving method `cacheable=true`. Its DML fails.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Wire reads, imperative writes."** Read and cache = wire. A click that saves = imperative. Apex saved while LDS is on screen = `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable`.

terms.say: Salesforce's own server code. You call it from a component when LDS can't do the job, like a custom query or logic.
Calling Apex yourself, like a normal function, when you choose, such as on a click. This is how you save data.
A tag that lets components call an Apex method. On a class property, it lets that value reach the browser.
Means the browser may keep and reuse the answer. So the method must only read. Saving data inside it fails. @wire needs it.
Apex commands that change the database: insert, update, delete. Like writing in the record book, not just reading it.
An answer that arrives later. An imperative Apex call returns one. You wait for it, then use the result or catch the error.
Asks a wired Apex method to fetch fresh data. Give it the whole wired result, not just result.data, or nothing happens.
Tells LDS a record changed somewhere else, like in Apex. LDS fetches it again and updates every component showing it.
The whole object a wire hands you, holding data and error together. refreshApex needs this exact object.

lessons.title: Lifecycle hooks & error handling
lessons.objective: Describe the Lightning Web Component lifecycle and implement error handling in components and their Apex controllers

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A component has a life. It's built, put on the page, drawn, and later removed. **Lifecycle hooks** are methods LWC calls at each step. You use them to set things up and clean up after. Good error handling means users see a clear message, not a crash.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a **hotel stay**. `constructor`: the room is built. `connectedCallback`: you check in. `renderedCallback`: housekeeping after every change. `disconnectedCallback`: you check out and take your things. Where it stops: housekeeping runs after **every** render, not once a day.

cards.title: The lifecycle in order
items: `constructor()`: call `super()` first. Public properties aren't set yet, so don't touch them
`connectedCallback()`: put on the page (inserted into the DOM). Runs parent first, then child
`renderedCallback()`: after each render. Runs child first, then parent
`disconnectedCallback()`: removed from the DOM. Clean up here
`errorCallback(error, stack)`: catches errors from child components

cards.body: `renderedCallback` **runs after EVERY render.** Guard one-time work, like setting up a chart library, with a flag: `if (this.chartReady) return;`. Don't change tracked state there either, or the component re-renders in a loop.

cards.title: Set up and clean up in pairs
cards.body: **Connect and disconnect come in pairs.** Whatever you add in `connectedCallback`, remove in `disconnectedCallback`: window listeners, LMS subscriptions, timers. Skip the cleanup and you leak memory as users move between pages.

cards.title: `errorCallback` = error boundary
cards.body: `errorCallback` is a **safety net** for children. It catches errors thrown in the lifecycle hooks or rendering of **child** components. It does **not** catch the component's own errors. So put it in a parent wrapper, and show a fallback screen when it fires.

cards.title: Friendly Apex errors
cards.body: Catches the DML error and throws `AuraHandledException`, so the browser gets your clear message and no stack trace.

cards.title: Error and loading gotchas
items: Apex errors: read the message from `error.body.message`
`getRecord` (UI API read) errors: `error.body` is an **array**. Join each item's message
`ShowToastEvent` doesn't work in **LWR** Experience Cloud sites. Use `lightning/toast`
File inside a zip static resource: `RESOURCE + '/path/file.js'`, **with the slash**
`ltng:require` and `loadScript` don't spot each other, so the same file can run twice

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Plug in, unplug."** What `connectedCallback` adds, `disconnectedCallback` removes. And a parent's `errorCallback` catches its children, never itself.

terms.say: Methods LWC calls by itself at each step of a component's life: built, put on the page, drawn, and removed.
Runs first, when the component is built. Call super() first. Public properties aren't set yet, so don't use them here.
Runs when the component is put on the page. Good for loading data or adding listeners. The parent runs first, then the child.
Runs after every render, child first, then parent. Guard one-time work with a flag, and don't change watched data there, or it loops.
Runs when the component is removed from the page. Clean up here: remove listeners, stop timers, unsubscribe.
A safety net in a parent. It catches errors from its child components, never its own. Show a fallback screen when it fires.
The browser's tree of everything on the page. A component inserted into the DOM is on the page; removed from it, it's gone.
An Apex error made for components. Throw it with a clear message, and the user sees that message instead of technical details.
Shows a small pop-up message, called a toast. It doesn't work in LWR sites, a newer kind of Experience Cloud site. Use lightning/toast there.
A file you upload to Salesforce, like a script or a zip. Components load it from there. For a file inside a zip, add a slash and its path.

lessons.title: Talking between components
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement the correct method to communicate events through Lightning Web Components or Aura Components

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Components often need to share news. A parent tells a child what to show. A child tells its parent what was clicked. Two strangers on the same page need to stay in sync. Each case has its own **channel**, and picking the right one is a favorite exam question.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a house. Parents **hand notes down** to kids (`@api`). Kids **shout up the stairs** (events). Neighbors use the **street mailbox** (Lightning Message Service). Where it stops: a shout normally stops at the first closed door, the component's shadow boundary.

cards.title: Pick the channel
items: Parent to child: `@api` property or `@api` method
Child to parent: `CustomEvent`
Unrelated components, even across LWC, Aura and Visualforce: **Lightning Message Service (LMS)**

cards.title: Fire and handle
cards.body: The child fires `'select'` with its data in `detail`; the parent listens with `onselect` ("on" + event name).

Event names: **no uppercase letters, no spaces**. HTML attributes ignore case, so `itemSelected` breaks and `itemselected` works. Use underscores to split words if you must. Don't start the name with "on".

cards.title: `bubbles` / `composed` (both default false)
items: false/false: only the child's host element hears it. Recommended
`bubbles:true`: travels up the page, but **stops at the shadow boundary** (the wall around each component's insides)
`bubbles` + `composed` true: crosses every shadow boundary and leaks into everyone's DOM. Avoid it. Better: each parent re-fires its own event

cards.title: Lightning Message Service
cards.body: Publishes and subscribes on a shared channel; the channel itself is `LightningMessageChannel` metadata.

cards.title: LMS and Aura mixing rules
items: Hear messages in background tabs: subscribe with `{ scope: APPLICATION_SCOPE }`
Aura uses `<lightning:messageChannel>` and finds it by its `aura:id`
Mobile app: LMS works for Aura and LWC, **not Visualforce**
Aura reads LWC event data with `event.getParam('key')`
Aura can call only `@api` LWC methods, and not during init

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "Down = `@api`, Up = event, Sideways = LMS."

terms.say: Lets a parent hand data down to a child, or call a child's method. Like a note passed down from parent to kid.
How a child tells its parent something happened. It fires an event with a name and its data. The parent listens with on plus the name.
The part of an event that carries its data. The parent reads it as event.detail.
A shared message channel for the page. Components that aren't related, even LWC, Aura and Visualforce, can send and hear messages on it.
The wall around each component's insides. An event that bubbles stops here, unless composed is also true.
Says if an event travels up through the parents. It's false by default. True lets it go up, but only to the shadow boundary.
Says if an event may cross shadow boundaries. With bubbles also true, it travels out of every component. Best avoided.
The metadata that creates a message channel. Senders and listeners name the same channel to talk.
A subscribe option for LMS. The component then also hears messages while it sits in a background tab.

lessons.title: Surfacing components: App Builder, Flow, actions & more
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, surface Lightning Web Components and Aura Components on Lightning pages, Visualforce pages, Quick Actions, Flows and Experience Cloud

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Building a component is half the job. Next you decide **where it can appear**: record pages, flows, quick actions, phones, Experience Cloud sites. A small config file, `js-meta.xml`, lists those places. Admins then drag the component onto pages in **Lightning App Builder**, the drag-and-drop page editor.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: `js-meta.xml` is the **label on a plug**. It lists the sockets the component fits: record page, flow screen, quick action. `isExposed` is the on switch. Where it stops: some sockets also need code, like `@api invoke()` for an action with no screen.

cards.title: `js-meta.xml`
cards.body: Allows Account record pages and flow screens; each property must match an `@api` field in the JS.

cards.title: Common targets (places it can go)
items: `lightning__AppPage` / `RecordPage` / `HomePage`
`lightning__RecordAction` (quick action)
`lightning__FlowScreen`
`lightning__UtilityBar`, `lightning__Tab`
`lightningCommunity__Page` + `lightningCommunity__Default` (Experience Builder)

cards.title: Quick actions and flows
items: Quick action: target `lightning__RecordAction`. `actionType` `ScreenAction` opens a modal. Close it with `CloseActionScreenEvent` from `lightning/actions`
`actionType` `Action` is headless (no screen). The platform calls your `@api invoke()`
Flow output: dispatch `new FlowAttributeChangeEvent('prop', value)` from `lightning/flowSupport`
Block Next: `@api validate()` returning `{ isValid, errorMessage }`

cards.title: `NavigationMixin`
cards.body: Opens the standard New Contact form on desktop, mobile and sites alike; never use `window.location` (`GenerateUrl` returns a Promise).

cards.title: Devices and other places
items: Device rules go inside each `targetConfig`: `Large` (desktop) and `Small` (phone)
In JS, `@salesforce/client/formFactor` returns `Large`, `Medium` or `Small`
LWC on a Visualforce page: **Lightning Out**. Add `<apex:includeLightning/>` and an app that extends `ltng:outApp`, then call `$Lightning.use()` and `$Lightning.createComponent()`
Just "show this field when…"? Use **Dynamic Forms** or **Dynamic Actions**, no code

cards.body: `isExposed` **false means invisible.** The component won't appear in App Builder at all, whatever targets you list. Second trap: LWC App Builder properties live in `js-meta.xml`. A `.design` file is for **Aura** only.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Expose it, target it, configure it."** `isExposed` true, then `<targets>`, then `<targetConfigs>` for properties, objects and devices.

terms.say: A component's config file. It says if the component is exposed, where it can go, and which properties admins can set.
Salesforce's drag-and-drop page editor. Admins place exposed components on record, app and home pages.
The on switch in js-meta.xml. If false, admins can't use the component in App Builder or Flow, whatever targets you list.
The list of places a component may go, like record pages, flow screens or quick actions.
Settings for one target: properties admins can set, which objects it works on, and which devices.
A button on a record page. A ScreenAction opens a pop-up with your component. An Action with no screen just runs your code.
With no screen. A headless quick action just calls your @api invoke() method when clicked.
An event a flow screen component fires to send a new value back to the flow.
Lets you show Lightning components outside Lightning pages, like on a Visualforce page.
An admin tool that shows or hides fields on a record page by rules, with no code.

lessons.title: Aura: still on the exam
lessons.objective: Given a set of requirements, select the appropriate Lightning Web Component, Aura Component, or Visualforce solution and describe its benefits

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Aura** is the older Lightning component framework. LWC replaced it, but many orgs still run Aura, and the exam still asks about it. You need to know how Aura talks, how it mixes with LWC, and when only Aura or Visualforce can do the job.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of **nesting dolls**. A big Aura doll can hold a small LWC doll. A small LWC doll can never hold an Aura doll. Where it stops: real dolls don't talk, but the LWC inside can still send events out to the Aura around it.

cards.title: Nesting rule
cards.body: An **Aura component can contain an LWC**. An **LWC cannot contain an Aura component**. So migrate from the inside out. Rebuild the small inner pieces (the leaves) in LWC first, and keep Aura as the outer wrapper until last.

cards.title: Component event
cards.code:
<!-- child.cmp -->
<aura:registerEvent name="selectEvt" type="c:SelectEvent"/>

<!-- parent.cmp -->
<aura:handler name="selectEvt" event="c:SelectEvent"
              action="{!c.handleSelect}"/>
cards.body: A component event goes up to the containers (capture, then bubble), fired with `cmp.getEvent()`; the handler's name must match.

cards.title: Application event
cards.body: An application event is broadcast to every handler in the app; new builds usually use LMS instead.

cards.title: Aura cheat sheet
items: Run code on load: `<aura:handler name="init" value="{!this}" action="{!c.doInit}"/>`
Call Apex: `cmp.get('c.method')`, `setCallback`, then `$A.enqueueAction(action)`
Errors: `response.getError()` is an **array**, so read `errors[0].message`
Several scripts in one `ltng:require`: combine with `join()`, then run code in `afterScriptsLoaded`
Phone check: `$Browser.formFactor == 'PHONE'` or `$Browser.isPhone`

cards.title: When LWC can't do it
items: **PDF**: only Visualforce has `renderAs="pdf"`. Apex can save it with `getContentAsPDF()`
**Override a standard button** like New: wrap the LWC in Aura that implements `lightning:actionOverride`
Overrides for **Salesforce Classic** users: must be Visualforce
Show an LWC on an **outside, non-Salesforce site**: Lightning Out

cards.body: **Name or no name?** `<aura:handler name="...">` handles component events. Leave the name out for application events. Mix them up and the handler never fires.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Big doll holds small doll."** Aura holds LWC, never the reverse. A **named** handler catches component events; a **nameless** one catches application events.

terms.say: Salesforce's older Lightning component framework. LWC replaced it, but many orgs still use it, and the exam still asks about it.
Lightning Web Components, Salesforce's newer way to build components with standard web code. It replaced Aura.
An Aura event that travels up to the components around it, capture first, then bubble. Its handler needs a matching name.
An Aura event sent to every handler in the app, like a loudspeaker. Its handler has no name. New builds use LMS instead.
Puts an Aura server call in the queue to send. Without it, the Apex call never runs.
Gives an Aura server call the function to run when the answer comes back.
An Aura tag that loads outside script and style files from static resources. afterScriptsLoaded runs your code once they're ready.
A Visualforce page setting. renderAs="pdf" turns the page into a PDF, which only Visualforce can do.
An Aura interface that lets a component replace a standard button, like New. Wrap your LWC in it to override one.
Lets you show Lightning components outside Lightning, like on a Visualforce page or another website.

lessons.title: Visualforce controllers & view state
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use Visualforce standard controllers, custom controllers, extensions and StandardSetController

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Visualforce** is Salesforce's older page tech: HTML-like tags plus an Apex **controller**, the class that holds the page's data and actions. You pick the controller type by what you need. Standard behavior, a little extra, all custom, or a whole list of records.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of ordering **pizza**. Standard controller: the house pizza. Extension: the house pizza plus your topping. Custom controller: you bring every ingredient. `StandardSetController`: a party order of many pizzas. Where it stops: the custom one runs in **system mode**, so you add sharing yourself.

cards.title: Controller menu
items: **Standard controller**: standard actions and behavior. Runs in **user mode** (respects the user's access)
**Extension**: adds to or overrides a standard or custom controller
**Custom controller**: all your own logic. Runs in **system mode** (ignores the user's access), so declare it `with sharing`
`StandardSetController`: works on lists of records (list views, mass actions)

cards.title: Extension constructor
cards.body: The extension receives the standard controller and grabs the current record (a list page passes `ApexPages.StandardSetController` instead).

cards.title: Mass action on list view
cards.body: `recordSetVar` makes this a list page; in the extension, `ssc.getSelected()` returns the records ticked in the list view.

cards.title: Controller gotchas
items: The standard controller loads only fields **used on the page**. Need more? `std.addFields()` in the constructor, or a hidden field with `rendered="false"`
`StandardSetController` holds **10,000** records. A bigger query locator throws a `LimitException`; a bigger List is cut short
Custom controller save errors: catch the `DmlException`, call `ApexPages.addMessages(ex)`, and add `<apex:pageMessages/>`
Zip static resource file: `URLFOR($Resource.Name, 'path/file.js')`

cards.title: View state: 170 KB max
cards.body: **View state** is the page's memory. Visualforce keeps controller data in a hidden form field and sends it on every postback (each trip back to the server). The max is **170 KB**, and you can't raise it. Shrink it: mark data you don't need to keep `transient`, query fewer fields, and load read-only data with **JavaScript remoting**.
With `extensions="ExtA,ExtB"`, if both define the same method, the **leftmost** one (`ExtA`) wins. Not the last one. It also beats the standard controller's method with the same name.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Transient = travel light.** Transient and static variables are **not** saved in view state. Lighter bag, faster page.

terms.say: Salesforce's older page tech: HTML-like tags plus an Apex class. Still used for PDFs and Salesforce Classic.
The Apex class behind a Visualforce page. It holds the page's data and what its buttons do.
Salesforce's ready-made controller for an object. It gives save, edit and delete for free, and respects the user's access.
An extra Apex class that adds to or overrides a controller's methods. Like the house pizza plus your own topping.
An Apex class you write with all the page's logic. It runs in system mode, so add with sharing yourself.
Code runs with full power, ignoring the user's object and field permissions. Sharing is ignored too, unless the class says with sharing.
An Apex class keyword. It makes the code respect sharing, so users only get records they may see. It doesn't check fields.
A controller for lists of records, like a list view or mass action. It holds up to 10,000 records.
The page's memory, kept in a hidden field and sent on every trip to the server. The max is 170 KB, and it can't be raised.
A keyword for variables the page doesn't need to remember. They aren't saved in view state, so the page stays light.

lessons.title: Visualforce AJAX: partial refresh & async
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use Visualforce to perform actions, partial page refreshes and asynchronous operations

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Reloading the whole page on every click is slow. **AJAX** lets a Visualforce page talk to the server and redraw just one part. That's a **partial page refresh**. Visualforce gives you ready-made tags for it, plus **JavaScript remoting** for fast, direct calls.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A partial refresh is like **swapping one tile in a mosaic** instead of rebuilding the wall. You name the tile with `rerender`. Where it stops: you can only swap a tile that's already on the wall. A part that wasn't drawn at page load has no spot to fill.

cards.title: AJAX toolbox
items: `apex:actionSupport`: adds AJAX to a component's browser event, like `onchange`
`apex:actionFunction`: makes a JS function that calls a controller action
`apex:actionPoller`: calls an action on a timer
`apex:actionStatus`: shows a "loading…" indicator
`apex:actionRegion`: sends and checks only the fields inside it
`rerender="id1,id2"`: redraws only those components

cards.body: You **can't rerender** a component that wasn't drawn (`rendered="false"`) when the page loaded. It isn't on the page to replace. Wrap it in an always-drawn `apex:outputPanel` and rerender the wrapper.

cards.title: `actionFunction`
cards.code:
<apex:actionFunction name="recalc" action="{!recalculate}"
                     rerender="totals">
  <apex:param name="qty" assignTo="{!qty}" value=""/>
</apex:actionFunction>
<!-- JS: recalc(5); -->
cards.body: Creates a JS function `recalc(5)` that sends the view state, runs `recalculate`, then redraws `totals`.

cards.title: JavaScript remoting
cards.body: Calls a `static` `@RemoteAction` straight from JS, sends **no view state**, and hands the result to a callback.

cards.title: Partial refresh gotchas
items: `immediate="true"` skips validation **and** skips saving typed values. Fine for Cancel, wrong for Recalculate
Show errors after a partial refresh: add `apex:pageMessages` to `rerender` too
Put `apex:actionFunction` after any iteration like `apex:repeat`, never inside it, but still inside `apex:form`
Slow callout? Return a **Continuation** so it doesn't count as a long-running request

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: `actionFunction` = "Visualforce does the redraw." Remoting = "JS does everything, fast and stateless."

terms.say: Talking to the server in the background, then redrawing only part of the page. No full reload.
Redrawing just one part of a page instead of the whole thing. Like swapping one tile in a mosaic.
Names which components to redraw, by id, after an action. A component that wasn't drawn at page load can't be rerendered.
Adds AJAX to a browser event on a component, like onchange. When it happens, a controller action runs.
Makes a JavaScript function that calls a controller action. Visualforce sends the view state and does the redraw.
Marks part of a form. Only the fields inside it are sent and checked when an action runs.
immediate="true" skips validation and doesn't save what the user typed. Good for Cancel, wrong when you need typed values.
Calling an Apex method straight from JavaScript. It's fast and sends no view state, but your JavaScript must update the page.
A tag on a static Apex method so JavaScript remoting can call it.
Lets a page wait for a slow outside web call without tying up the server. It doesn't count as a long-running request.

lessons.title: UI security: XSS, CSP, LWS & FLS
lessons.objective: Identify and prevent security vulnerabilities in Visualforce and Lightning components and enforce data access in their Apex controllers

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A page that shows user input can be tricked into running a stranger's code. That's **XSS** (cross-site scripting). Two more risks: a link that makes you do something you didn't mean to (**CSRF**), and Apex showing data the user shouldn't see. This lesson blocks all three.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Escaping is like **putting a note behind glass**. People can read it, but nobody can reach through and press buttons. Turning escaping off removes the glass. Where it stops: the glass must match the spot. HTML, JavaScript and URLs each need their own kind.

cards.title: XSS in Visualforce
cards.body: Merge fields like `{!comment}` are **HTML-escaped by default**: tags show as text, not code. `escape="false"` on `apex:outputText` turns that off, so user input can run as script. Never use it with data a user typed.

cards.title: Encode for the spot
items: Inside `<script>`: `JSENCODE()`
JS inside an HTML attribute (`onclick`): `JSINHTMLENCODE()`
Raw HTML output: `HTMLENCODE()`
In a URL: `URLENCODE()`

cards.title: CSRF: no saving on page load
cards.body: **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery) means another site makes a signed-in user's browser send a request. Visualforce forms carry an anti-CSRF token. But a page's `action` attribute runs on load, with no token check. So never do DML (delete, update) in a page action. Make the user click a confirm button.

cards.title: CSP in Lightning
cards.body: Lightning pages enforce **Content Security Policy (CSP)**, a rule list of what may load. Inline `<script>` tags and CDN scripts are blocked. Upload libraries as a **static resource** (5 MB each, 250 MB per org). Load them with `loadScript` / `loadStyle` from `lightning/platformResourceLoader`. To `fetch()` an outside API, add its domain as a **Trusted URL**.

cards.title: Lightning Web Security
cards.body: **LWS** replaces **Lightning Locker**. It puts each namespace in its own JavaScript sandbox and changes risky browser APIs ("distortions"). Unlike Locker, it lets components import modules from other namespaces. For user HTML in LWC, use `lightning-formatted-rich-text`, which cleans it. Never write user data to `innerHTML`.

LDS and base record components enforce CRUD and FLS. Your `@AuraEnabled` Apex does NOT, unless you make it. Use `WITH USER_MODE` in SOQL, `Security.stripInaccessible()`, or `AccessLevel.USER_MODE` for DML. Sharing keywords control **which records** only, not fields.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Glass, token, gate."** Glass: escape output (XSS). Token: no DML on page load (CSRF). Gate: `WITH USER_MODE` or `stripInaccessible` in Apex (FLS).

terms.say: Cross-site scripting. A stranger sneaks code into text your page shows, and the page runs it. Escaping the text stops it.
Turning special characters into plain text, so code shows as words and can't run. Like a note behind glass.
Escapes a value for use inside a script tag, so it can't break out and run as code.
Cross-site request forgery. Another site tricks a signed-in user's browser into sending a request, like a save. Visualforce forms carry a secret token to stop it.
Content Security Policy. A rule list of what a Lightning page may load. Inline scripts and scripts from outside sites are blocked.
An outside web address your org allows. Add one so your components may send requests to that site.
Lightning Web Security. It puts each namespace's code in its own sandbox and makes risky browser features safer. It replaces Lightning Locker.
The older security layer for Lightning components. It walls off each namespace, but blocks importing modules from other namespaces. LWS replaces it.
Telling Apex: act like the person using the app. Then it checks their object access, field access and sharing, all three.
A quiet cleaner. You hand it records, it removes fields the user may not touch, and gives back clean copies. No error.

flashcards.front: Does a plain LWC class field re-render the screen when it changes?
flashcards.back: Yes, when you give it a new value and the template uses it. Changing something inside an object or array needs `@track` or a new object.

flashcards.front: When do you still need `@track`?
flashcards.back: When you change a property inside a plain object, or an item in an array, without assigning a new one. `@track` makes LWC watch those inner changes.

flashcards.front: What does `@api` do?
flashcards.back: It makes a property or method public. The parent, App Builder or Flow can set the property. A parent can call the method through `querySelector`.

flashcards.front: Can a child change an `@api` object it received from its parent?
flashcards.back: No, it is read-only to the child. Copy it into a private field, or dispatch an event so the owner changes it.

flashcards.front: How do you make a wire parameter update when a property changes?
flashcards.back: Put a `$` in front of the property name, in quotes: `{ recordId: '$recordId' }`. The wire fetches again whenever that property changes.

flashcards.front: In `getRecord`, what is the difference between `fields` and `optionalFields`?
flashcards.back: If the user can't see a field in `fields`, the whole call errors. A field in `optionalFields` is just left out, with no error.

flashcards.front: Which `uiRecordApi` helper reads one field's value from a record?
flashcards.back: `getFieldValue(record, FIELD)`, using a field imported from `@salesforce/schema`. For the formatted, localized value, use `getFieldDisplayValue`.

flashcards.front: What does `getPicklistValues` need?
flashcards.back: A record type Id, often `defaultRecordTypeId` from `getObjectInfo`, and the field: `recordTypeId` plus `fieldApiName`.

flashcards.front: What must an Apex method have so an LWC can wire it?
flashcards.back: It must be `static`, `public` or `global`, and marked `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`. Cacheable methods can't do DML.

flashcards.front: What do you pass to `refreshApex`?
flashcards.back: The whole value the wire handed you (the result object with data and error), not `result.data`. It returns a Promise.

flashcards.front: Apex updated a record that LDS shows on screen. What do you call?
flashcards.back: `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable([{ recordId }])` from `lightning/uiRecordApi`. LDS then fetches the record again. It replaces `getRecordNotifyChange`.

flashcards.front: How do you send a friendly error message from Apex to an LWC?
flashcards.back: Catch the error and `throw new AuraHandledException(message)`. The LWC reads it from `error.body.message`.

flashcards.front: In what order do `connectedCallback` and `renderedCallback` run for parent and child?
flashcards.back: `connectedCallback` runs parent first, then child. `renderedCallback` runs child first, then parent.

flashcards.front: What does `errorCallback` catch?
flashcards.back: Errors from child (descendant) components, in their lifecycle hooks or rendering. Not the component's own errors. It is an error boundary.

flashcards.front: What are the default `bubbles` and `composed` values of a `CustomEvent`?
flashcards.back: Both are false: `bubbles: false`, `composed: false`. Only the host element of the component that fired it hears the event.

flashcards.front: What are the naming rules for LWC events?
flashcards.back: No uppercase letters and no spaces. Use underscores if needed. Don't start the name with "on". The handler attribute is on + eventname.

flashcards.front: When should you use Lightning Message Service?
flashcards.back: When components that aren't related must talk across the page, including LWC, Aura and Visualforce on the same Lightning page.

flashcards.front: Which LMS scope lets a subscriber hear messages from the whole app?
flashcards.back: `APPLICATION_SCOPE`, passed in the subscribe options. By default, a subscriber only hears messages while it is in the active area.

flashcards.front: Which target makes an LWC a quick action?
flashcards.back: `lightning__RecordAction`. Set `actionType` `ScreenAction` for a modal, or `Action` for a headless one that runs `@api invoke()`.

flashcards.front: How does a Flow screen LWC send a value back to the flow?
flashcards.back: Dispatch `new FlowAttributeChangeEvent('propName', value)` from `lightning/flowSupport`. The property must be `@api` and listed in the `targetConfig`.

flashcards.front: Which targets put an LWC in Experience Builder?
flashcards.back: `lightningCommunity__Page` makes it available in the builder. `lightningCommunity__Default` makes its properties editable there.

flashcards.front: How do you show an LWC on a Visualforce page?
flashcards.back: Use Lightning Out: `<apex:includeLightning/>`, an Aura app that extends `ltng:outApp`, then `$Lightning.use()` and `$Lightning.createComponent()`.

flashcards.front: Can an LWC contain an Aura component?
flashcards.back: No. Aura can contain LWC, but LWC can't contain Aura.

flashcards.front: How do Aura component events and application events differ?
flashcards.back: Component event: fired with `cmp.getEvent()`, handled by `aura:handler` whose name matches `registerEvent`. Application event: fired with `$A.get("e.c:Evt")`, handled by `aura:handler` with no name.

flashcards.front: How big can a Visualforce page's view state be?
flashcards.back: 170 KB at most. Shrink it with `transient` variables, smaller queries and JavaScript remoting.

flashcards.front: Two Visualforce extensions both define `save()`. Which one runs?
flashcards.back: The leftmost one in the `extensions` attribute.

flashcards.front: What does a list page extension's constructor take?
flashcards.back: An `ApexPages.StandardSetController`. The page itself uses `standardController` plus `recordSetVar`.

flashcards.front: How do `actionFunction` and JavaScript remoting differ?
flashcards.back: `actionFunction` sends the view state and can redraw parts of the page. Remoting calls a `static` `@RemoteAction` with no view state and returns the result to a JS callback.

flashcards.front: How do you use a merge field safely inside a `<script>` block?
flashcards.back: Wrap it in `JSENCODE()`, for example: `var n = '{!JSENCODE($CurrentPage.parameters.n)}';`

flashcards.front: How do you load a third-party JS library in an LWC?
flashcards.back: Upload it as a static resource and call `loadScript(this, resourceUrl)` from `lightning/platformResourceLoader`. CSP blocks CDN script tags.

flashcards.front: Does `@track` see changes inside a `Set`, `Map` or `Date`?
flashcards.back: No. LWC only watches plain objects and arrays. For a `Set`, `Map`, `Date` or class instance, assign a new one to re-render.

flashcards.front: How many records can a `StandardSetController` hold?
flashcards.back: 10,000. A query locator that returns more throws a `LimitException`. A List with more is cut down to 10,000.

flashcards.front: How do you stop `updateRecord` from overwriting someone else's newer save?
flashcards.back: Pass `clientOptions` `{ ifUnmodifiedSince: lastModifiedDate }`, with `LastModifiedDate` read through a wire adapter. If the record changed since, the update fails.

questions.q: A component shows `{count}` in its template. The class declares `count = 0;` with no decorator, and a button handler runs `this.count++`. What happens when the button is clicked?
options: It re-renders and shows the new value of `count`, since reassigned fields are reactive
Nothing changes on screen until `count` is decorated with `@track`, because primitive fields are not observed
Nothing changes on screen until `count` is decorated with `@api`
The template only updates if `count` is exposed through a getter
questions.explain: Giving a field a new value re-renders the component, if the template uses it. `this.count++` assigns a new value, so the screen shows it. No decorator is needed.
wrong: `@track` is only for changes inside an object or array, not for simple values like numbers.
`@api` makes a property public; it has nothing to do with reactivity.
No getter is needed, because the field itself is already reactive.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Reactivity

questions.q: A developer clicks the button that calls `handleClose()`, but the template that shows `{filters.status}` still says "Open". Which two changes would make the UI update? (Choose 2)
options: Decorate `filters` with `@api`
Call `this.render()` at the end of `handleClose()`
Decorate `filters` with `@track`
Assign a new object: `this.filters = { ...this.filters, status: 'Closed' };`
Move the assignment into `renderedCallback()`
questions.explain: LWC only notices when the field gets a new value, not when something inside it changes. `this.filters.status = 'Closed'` changes the inside, so it's missed. Either add `@track` to watch the inside, or assign a brand-new object.
wrong: `@api` makes the field public; it adds no deep watching, and a component shouldn't change its own public properties.
There is no supported `render()` call that forces a re-render.
Changing state in `renderedCallback` risks a render loop, and it's still an unwatched inside change.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Reactivity for Fields, Objects, and Arrays

questions.q: A component must show a contact's full name built from its `firstName` and `lastName` fields. What is the correct way to show it in the template?
options: Use `{firstName + ' ' + lastName}` directly in the template, like an Aura expression
Set a `fullName` field inside `renderedCallback()`
Define `get fullName()` in the class and reference `{fullName}`
Use an `@wire` decorator to combine the two fields
questions.explain: LWC templates don't allow expressions like `first + last`. Work out the value in a **getter** and show `{fullName}`. The getter runs again on every render, so it stays fresh.
wrong: Expressions aren't allowed in LWC templates; this fails to compile.
Setting state in `renderedCallback` triggers another render and risks an endless loop.
`@wire` brings in data from wire adapters; it doesn't combine local values.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Use Getters to Compute a Value

questions.q: A parent passes an Account object to a child through `<c-acct-editor record={acct}>`. The child declares `@api record` and runs `this.record.Name = this.newName` when the user types, which throws an error. What should the developer do?
options: Decorate `record` with `@track` in addition to `@api` so the child gets its own writable, deep-tracked copy
Move the assignment into the child's constructor
Use `JSON.stringify(this.record)` before assigning
Copy the object into a private field and edit the copy, or fire an event so the parent updates `acct`
questions.explain: A child can't change an object it got through `@api`, because the parent owns it. So the child edits its own copy, or sends an event asking the parent to change it. Think: data down, events up.
wrong: A field can't have both `@api` and `@track`, and that wouldn't make the parent's object writable.
Public properties aren't set yet in the constructor, and the object would still be read-only.
Turning the object into a string doesn't let the child change the original property.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Public Properties / Data Flow

questions.q: On an Account record page, a component must show Name, Industry and Phone as read-only values and respect each user's field-level security. The requirement is the least code possible. What should the developer use?
options: An `@AuraEnabled` Apex method that queries Name, Industry and Phone, shown in a custom HTML template
`lightning-record-form` with `object-api-name`, `record-id`, `fields` and `mode="readonly"`
A Visualforce page embedded in an iframe
`getRecord` with a custom template of `lightning-formatted-text` elements
questions.explain: For read-only fields with the least code, use a ready-made form. `lightning-record-form` with `mode="readonly"` uses LDS, so it enforces CRUD, FLS and sharing with no Apex.
wrong: This needs more code, and Apex doesn't enforce FLS unless you code it yourself.
An iframed Visualforce page adds complexity and fits Lightning Experience poorly.
This works, but it needs much more code than one base component.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Compare Base Components (lightning-record-form)

questions.q: A component calls `getRecord` with `fields: [NAME_FIELD, RATING_FIELD]`. Users without field-level access to `Account.Rating` see an error, and the Name is not shown either. What is the best fix?
options: Mark the Apex controller as `without sharing`
Use `layoutTypes: ['Full']` instead of `fields`
Move `RATING_FIELD` into `optionalFields`
Wrap the `@wire` decorator in a try/catch block
questions.explain: In `getRecord`, one field the user can't see in `fields` makes the whole call fail. Move Rating to `optionalFields`, where a hidden field is simply left out. Then Name shows again.
wrong: `getRecord` uses LDS, not Apex, and sharing doesn't control field-level security anyway.
Layout types change which fields come back; they don't handle missing field access predictably.
Wire errors arrive in the `error` property; they're never thrown, so try/catch can't catch them.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: getRecord

questions.q: A developer needs a two-column custom form to create Case records. Before saving, the component must set Origin to "Web" without showing that field to the user. Which approach meets this?
options: `lightning-record-form` with `mode="edit"` and an `onsuccess` handler that sets Origin
`lightning-record-view-form` with a `lightning-output-field` for each field, plus a hidden `lightning-output-field` for Origin set to Web
A `getRecord` wire adapter with a `lightning-input` for each field
`lightning-record-edit-form` with `onsubmit`: call `preventDefault()`, add Origin to `event.detail.fields`, then `submit(fields)`
questions.explain: To change values before a save with your own layout, use `lightning-record-edit-form`. Its submit event lets you stop the save, add Origin to the fields, and call `submit(fields)`.
wrong: `onsuccess` fires after the save, which is too late, and record-form gives little layout control.
The view form is read-only; it can't create records, and output fields can't set values.
`getRecord` only reads; saving would still need `createRecord` and hand-built field handling.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Override Default Behaviors (lightning-record-edit-form)

questions.q: A team is choosing between Lightning Data Service and custom Apex for a set of record components. Which two statements about Lightning Data Service are true? (Choose 2)
options: It refreshes its cache automatically when an Apex method updates the same record
Records are cached and shared, so when one LDS component saves a record, other LDS components that show it update
It enforces CRUD, field-level security and sharing for the running user
It needs an `@AuraEnabled` Apex method to read field values
`updateRecord` can update thousands of records in one bulk call
questions.explain: LDS keeps one shared copy of each record in the browser, so its components stay in sync. It also runs with the user's own permissions: CRUD, FLS and sharing.
wrong: LDS can't see Apex DML; you must call `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable`.
LDS reads records through the UI API, with no Apex at all.
`updateRecord` saves one record per call; big bulk changes belong in Apex.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Lightning Data Service

questions.q: A developer adds `@wire(getOpenCases)` to an LWC. The Apex method is `public static` and annotated `@AuraEnabled`, but the component fails to load the data. What change is needed?
options: Make the method `global`
Change the annotation to `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`
Add the `@RemoteAction` annotation
Decorate the property with `@track`
questions.explain: Only read-only, cacheable Apex can be wired. The method needs `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`. Without it, you must call the method imperatively.
wrong: `public` is already enough for an `@AuraEnabled` method.
`@RemoteAction` is for Visualforce JavaScript remoting, not LWC.
`@track` has nothing to do with whether Apex can be wired.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Wire Apex Methods to Lightning Web Components

questions.q: An `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)` method creates a Task record and returns the new Id. The LWC calls it imperatively when a button is clicked. What is the result, and what is the fix?
options: It fails at runtime: cacheable methods cannot do DML. Remove `cacheable=true` and keep the imperative call
It works, but later clicks return the cached Id instead of creating a Task. Add `@track` to the result to avoid stale values
It fails because imperative calls must use `@wire`. Switch to `@wire`
It works only when the class is declared `without sharing`
questions.explain: A cacheable method must only read, so DML inside it fails at runtime. A method that creates a Task can't be cacheable. Remove `cacheable=true` and keep the imperative call.
wrong: The DML itself fails, and `@track` has no control over the cache.
Imperative calls are exactly the right way to call methods that aren't cacheable.
Sharing doesn't lift the no-DML rule for cacheable methods.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Call Apex Methods Imperatively

questions.q: After `saveContact()` succeeds, the contact list does not refresh, and `refreshApex` does nothing. What should the developer change?
options: Mark `saveContact` as `cacheable=true` so it shares the wire cache with `getContacts` and refreshes it on save
Call `getContacts` imperatively inside `renderedCallback()`
Decorate `contacts` with `@track` so `refreshApex` can see changes
Keep the whole provisioned result (`this.wiredResult = result`) and pass that to `refreshApex`
questions.explain: `refreshApex` needs the exact object the wire handed over, the one holding both data and error. Passing just the data array refreshes nothing. So keep the whole result and pass that.
wrong: A method that does DML can never be cacheable.
This calls Apex again on every render, which is wasteful.
Reactivity isn't the problem; `refreshApex` got the wrong value.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Refresh the Cache When Using @wire

questions.q: An LWC calls an imperative Apex method that updates the Account's Rating. A `lightning-record-form` on the same record page still shows the old Rating. Which two approaches are recommended? (Choose 2)
options: After the Apex promise resolves, call `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable([{ recordId: this.recordId }])`
Mark the Apex method `cacheable=true`
Use `updateRecord` from `lightning/uiRecordApi` instead of Apex for this single-record update
Call `refreshApex(this.recordId)`
Reload the page with `window.location.reload()` after the Apex promise resolves to show the new Rating
questions.explain: LDS can't see changes Apex makes. So either tell it with `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable`, or save through LDS itself with `updateRecord`, which updates the shared cache directly.
wrong: Cacheable methods can't do DML.
`refreshApex` refreshes wired Apex results, not LDS records, and `recordId` isn't a provisioned value.
A full page reload is poor UX and isn't the supported pattern.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: notifyRecordUpdateAvailable

questions.q: A component adds a window resize listener. Users report memory leaks after moving between pages. Where should the listener be added and removed?
options: Add it in the constructor and remove it in `renderedCallback()`
Add it in `renderedCallback()` and never remove it
Add it in `connectedCallback()` and remove it in `disconnectedCallback()`
Add it in `errorCallback()` and remove it in `connectedCallback()`
questions.explain: Set up global things when the component arrives, and remove them when it leaves. `connectedCallback` runs on insert and `disconnectedCallback` on removal. They're the matching pair for a window listener.
wrong: `renderedCallback` runs after every render, so the listener would be removed at the wrong times.
This adds a new listener on every render and never removes them, so they leak.
`errorCallback` catches child errors; it isn't for setup.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Lifecycle Hooks

questions.q: A developer loads a charting library with `loadScript` and draws a chart into a `<div lwc:dom="manual">` inside `renderedCallback()`. The chart is drawn again every time any property changes. What is the best fix?
options: Move the code into the constructor, which runs once per component instance, before any property changes
Add a boolean guard such as `chartInitialized` so the setup only runs once
Call `loadScript` from `disconnectedCallback()`
Decorate the chart field with `@api`
questions.explain: `renderedCallback` runs after every render, not once. So one-time work, like setting up a chart library, needs a guard flag such as `chartInitialized`.
wrong: The template hasn't rendered in the constructor, so the div doesn't exist yet.
`disconnectedCallback` runs when the component is removed, not when it loads.
`@api` has no effect on how often `renderedCallback` runs.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Use Third-Party JavaScript Libraries

questions.q: When a DML error occurs in an `@AuraEnabled` method, users see a generic "Script-thrown exception" message. The business wants a clear, custom message in the LWC toast. What should the developer do?
options: In Apex, catch it and `throw new AuraHandledException('clear message')`; in JS, read `error.body.message`
Return `null` from the method and check for `null` in JS
Use `System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, message)` so the message shows in the browser console and the toast
Wrap the imperative call in `errorCallback()`
questions.explain: To show your own message instead of a generic one, Apex must hand it over on purpose. Catch the error and throw `AuraHandledException`. The LWC reads it from `error.body.message`.
wrong: Returning `null` hides the error and tells the user nothing.
`System.debug` writes to debug logs, never to the browser or a toast.
`errorCallback` catches child component errors, not Apex errors from a promise.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Handle Errors / Apex Developer Guide: AuraHandledException

questions.q: A dashboard holds six child LWCs. If any child throws an error while rendering, the dashboard must show a friendly fallback panel and log the stack. Where should the developer put this logic?
options: A try/catch block in each child's `connectedCallback()`
`errorCallback()` in each child component
A `window.onerror` handler in the dashboard's `renderedCallback()` that swaps in the fallback panel and logs the stack
`errorCallback(error, stack)` in the parent dashboard, which sets a flag to render the fallback
questions.explain: `errorCallback` is a safety net for children, never for the component itself. It catches errors from descendants, so it belongs in the parent dashboard. There it can show the fallback and log the stack.
wrong: This misses rendering errors and repeats the same code in every child.
A component's `errorCallback` doesn't catch its own errors.
Global handlers don't fit the LWC model and run into security limits.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: errorCallback()

questions.q: A child component shows a list of products. When the user clicks one, its parent must receive the product Id. What should the developer do?
options: Publish the Id on a Lightning Message Service channel that the parent subscribes to in `connectedCallback()`
Dispatch a `CustomEvent` with the Id in `detail`, and listen with an `on<eventname>` attribute in the parent
Set an `@api` property on the parent from the child
Store the Id in `sessionStorage` and poll it from the parent
questions.explain: Children talk to their parent with events. The child dispatches a `CustomEvent` with the Id in `detail`. The parent listens with an `on<eventname>` attribute in its template.
wrong: LMS is for unrelated components; it's overkill for a parent and child.
A child can't set its parent's public properties; data only flows down.
Polling `sessionStorage` is a fragile anti-pattern.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Communicate with Events

questions.q: A child runs `this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('itemSelected'))`. The parent markup is `<c-item onitemSelected={handle}></c-item>`, but `handle` never runs. What is the fix?
options: Set `bubbles: true` on the event
Set `composed: true` on the event
Rename the event to `itemselected` and use `onitemselected` in the parent markup
Add a handler in the parent with `this.template.addEventListener('itemSelected')`
questions.explain: HTML attribute names ignore case, so LWC event names must be all lowercase. Rename the event to `itemselected` and listen with `onitemselected`.
wrong: The parent listens right on the child's host element, so bubbling isn't needed.
Crossing shadow boundaries isn't the problem here.
The uppercase name is still wrong, and the template listens on the wrong node.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Create and Dispatch Events

questions.q: A Lightning app page holds a Visualforce page, an Aura component and an LWC in separate regions. When a record is selected in the LWC, the other two must react. What should the developer use?
options: Lightning Message Service with a custom message channel
A `CustomEvent` with `bubbles: true` and `composed: true`
An Aura application event fired from the LWC
An `@api` method on the Visualforce page
questions.explain: Visualforce, Aura and LWC in separate page regions aren't related in the DOM. Lightning Message Service is the supported way for them to talk. It uses a custom message channel.
wrong: DOM events can't reach a Visualforce iframe or unrelated components.
An LWC can't fire Aura application events directly.
A Visualforce page can't expose `@api` methods.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Communicate Across the DOM with Lightning Message Service

questions.q: `c-grandparent`'s template contains `<c-child onnotify={handleNotify}>`. `c-child`'s template contains `<c-grandchild>`, which dispatches the event below. `handleNotify` never runs. Why, and what is the recommended fix?
questions.code:
// grandchild.js
this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('notify', { bubbles: true }));
options: The event name is invalid. Rename it to `onNotify`
`composed` is false, so the event stops at `c-child`'s shadow boundary; `c-child` should re-fire its own event
`bubbles` must be false for parents to listen
The grandparent must call `this.template.addEventListener('notify', ...)` in its constructor to catch deeper events
questions.explain: An event with `composed: false` stops at the next shadow boundary, here `c-child`'s. The clean fix is for `c-child` to re-fire its own event. `composed: true` also works, but it leaks the event everywhere, so it's discouraged.
wrong: Event names must not start with "on" and shouldn't have uppercase letters.
Bubbling isn't what stops the event; the shadow boundary is.
Child elements don't exist yet in the constructor, and the boundary would still block it.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Configure Event Propagation

questions.q: An LWC must be available in Lightning App Builder only on Account record pages. What is the correct configuration in its `js-meta.xml`?
options: `isExposed` true, target `lightning__AppPage`
`isExposed` false, target `lightning__RecordPage`, and a `targetConfig` for `lightning__RecordPage` listing `<object>Account</object>`
`isExposed` true, target `lightning__RecordPage`, and a `targetConfig` for it with `<object>Account</object>`
`isExposed` true, target `lightningCommunity__Page` with objects Account
questions.explain: To show up in App Builder, a component must be exposed and list where it fits. Set `isExposed` true, add the `lightning__RecordPage` target, and limit it with `<object>Account</object>`.
wrong: An App Page isn't a record page.
With `isExposed` false, the component never appears in App Builder.
`lightningCommunity__Page` is for Experience Builder pages.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: XML Configuration File Elements

questions.q: Admins must be able to set a component's heading text and maximum row count in Lightning App Builder. Which two steps are required? (Choose 2)
options: Declare `@api heading` and `@api maxRows` in the JS class
Create a `.design` file for the LWC
Add `<property>` elements for `heading` and `maxRows` in a `targetConfig` in `js-meta.xml`
Decorate the fields with `@track`
Store `heading` and `maxRows` in a custom metadata type that App Builder reads at design time
questions.explain: App Builder settings for an LWC need two matching parts. Declare `<property>` elements in a `targetConfig` in `js-meta.xml`. Each one must match an `@api` property in the class.
wrong: `.design` files are for Aura components, not LWC.
`@track` doesn't make a property public.
Custom metadata doesn't create App Builder properties.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Configure a Component for Lightning App Builder

questions.q: A button in an LWC must open the standard "New Contact" form. The solution must work in Lightning Experience and the Salesforce mobile app. What should the developer do?
options: Set `window.location` to `'/003/e'`
Use an `<a href="/lightning/o/Contact/new">` link, the Lightning Experience URL that opens the standard New Contact form
Dispatch a `CustomEvent` named `navigate`
Use `NavigationMixin` and `this[NavigationMixin.Navigate]` with type `standard__objectPage`, Contact and `actionName` `new`
questions.explain: Navigate with page references, never hard-coded URLs, so it works everywhere. `NavigationMixin` with `standard__objectPage` and `actionName: 'new'` opens the New Contact form on desktop, mobile and Experience Cloud.
wrong: A hard-coded Classic URL breaks in containers and on mobile.
A hard-coded URL is fragile and skips the navigation service.
A custom event doesn't navigate anywhere.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Navigate to Pages, Records, and Lists

questions.q: A custom LWC on a Flow screen lets the user pick a warehouse. The flow must use the picked warehouse Id in later elements. Which two steps are required? (Choose 2)
options: Publish the Id on a Lightning Message Service channel, and read it in later flow elements as a screen output
Declare an `@api warehouseId` property and list it as a `<property>` in the `lightning__FlowScreen` `targetConfig`
Dispatch `FlowNavigationFinishEvent` with the Id
Return the Id from `connectedCallback()`
Dispatch `FlowAttributeChangeEvent('warehouseId', id)` from `lightning/flowSupport` when a warehouse is picked
questions.explain: A flow reads outputs only from properties declared for the flow screen target. So declare `@api warehouseId` as a `<property>`, and fire `FlowAttributeChangeEvent` when it changes.
wrong: Flow doesn't read LMS messages as screen outputs.
`FlowNavigationFinishEvent` ends the flow; it doesn't set output values.
Lifecycle hook return values are ignored.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Configure a Component for Flow Screens

questions.q: In an Aura app, a child component must notify only the component that contains it when a row is selected. Which mechanism fits best?
options: A component event registered with `aura:registerEvent` and fired with `cmp.getEvent()`
An application event fired with `$A.get()`
Lightning Message Service with `APPLICATION_SCOPE`, using `lightning:messageChannel` in the parent
A platform event
questions.explain: To tell only the containing component, use an event that climbs the containment tree. That's a component event, registered with `aura:registerEvent` and fired with `cmp.getEvent()`.
wrong: Application events reach every handler in the app, which is too broad.
LMS is for unrelated components across the DOM.
Platform events are server-side messaging, not UI messaging.
questions.source: Lightning Aura Components Developer Guide: Component Events

questions.q: An Aura component must broadcast that a record changed to any component in the app that has a handler for `c:RecordChanged`. Which client-side code fires it correctly?
options: `var e = cmp.getEvent('RecordChanged'); e.fire();`
`var e = $A.get('e.c:RecordChanged'); e.setParams({ recordId: id }); e.fire();`
`this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('recordchanged'));`
`$A.enqueueAction('e.c:RecordChanged');`
questions.explain: A broadcast to the whole app is an application event. Get it with `$A.get('e.c:RecordChanged')`, add data with `setParams`, then call `fire()`.
wrong: `cmp.getEvent` fires a component event registered under that name, not a broadcast.
This is LWC syntax for DOM events.
`enqueueAction` queues server actions, not events.
questions.source: Lightning Aura Components Developer Guide: Fire Application Events

questions.q: A team has a large Aura component and wants to rebuild one of its sections as a new LWC without rewriting the whole thing. What is the supported approach?
options: Put the Aura component inside the new LWC's template
It is not possible. The whole Aura component must be rewritten
Embed the new LWC inside the existing Aura component's markup
Load the Aura component in the LWC with `loadScript`
questions.explain: Aura can hold an LWC, but an LWC can't hold Aura. So migrate from the inside out. Put the new LWC inside the existing Aura component.
wrong: An LWC can't contain an Aura component.
Aura and LWC work together, so step-by-step migration is supported.
`loadScript` loads JS libraries from static resources, not components.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Migrate Aura Components / Compose Aura Components from LWC

questions.q: The child fires its component event, but the parent's `handleSelect` never runs. What is wrong?
questions.code:
<!-- child.cmp -->
<aura:registerEvent name="selectEvt" type="c:SelectEvent"/>
<!-- childController.js -->
var evt = cmp.getEvent("selectEvt");
evt.setParams({ rowId: id });
evt.fire();

<!-- parent.cmp -->
<aura:handler event="c:SelectEvent" action="{!c.handleSelect}"/>
<c:child/>
options: The child must use `$A.get('e.c:selectEvt')` to fire the event, since `cmp.getEvent()` only reaches the child
`setParams` must be called after `fire()`
The parent must register the event as well
The `aura:handler` lacks `name="selectEvt"`, so it only handles application events
questions.explain: A component event handler must carry a `name` that matches the `aura:registerEvent` name. Without `name="selectEvt"`, Aura treats it as an application event handler, so it never fires.
wrong: `$A.get` is for application events; the child rightly fires a component event.
Parameters must be set before the event fires, not after.
Only the component that fires the event registers it.
questions.source: Lightning Aura Components Developer Guide: Handling Component Events

questions.q: A Visualforce page for Opportunity must keep the standard Save and Cancel behavior and add one custom "Calculate Discount" action. What is the most efficient approach?
options: A custom controller that rebuilds `save()` and `cancel()` with DML and `PageReference` logic
A `StandardSetController`
The Opportunity standard controller plus an extension that adds the method
A JavaScript remoting class only
questions.explain: To keep the standard actions and add one more, extend the standard controller. An extension adds the Calculate Discount method and keeps Save and Cancel for free.
wrong: Rebuilding the standard actions by hand is wasted effort.
`StandardSetController` is for lists of records.
Remoting doesn't give you the standard actions.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Building a Controller Extension

questions.q: Sales managers want to select several Accounts in a list view and click a button that sets Rating to "Hot" on the selected records. How should the Visualforce page be built?
options: `standardController` plus `recordSetVar`, and an extension that takes `StandardSetController` and uses `getSelected()`
`standardController="Account"` and an extension that takes `ApexPages.StandardController` and calls `getRecord()` on it
A custom controller that queries every Account
An `apex:actionPoller` that updates the records
questions.explain: A page that works on the user's list view selection is a list page. `recordSetVar` makes it one. The extension's `StandardSetController` then returns the ticked records through `getSelected()`.
wrong: `StandardController` works on one record and can't see the list view selection.
Querying every Account ignores what the user selected.
A poller runs actions on a timer and can't see the selection.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Standard List Controllers / StandardSetController

questions.q: A Visualforce page fails with "Maximum view state size limit exceeded". The controller holds a large list that is used only to draw a read-only table. Which two changes reduce view state? (Choose 2)
options: Make the list variable `public`
Mark the list as `transient`
Raise the view state limit in Session Settings
Load the read-only data with JavaScript remoting instead of storing it in the controller
Move the table inside an `apex:form`
questions.explain: View state is the page's saved memory, so keep big read-only data out of it. **Transient** variables aren't saved in view state. Data loaded through JavaScript remoting isn't stored there either.
wrong: Access modifiers don't change what gets saved in view state.
The 170 KB limit can't be changed.
View state comes from `apex:form`, so this wouldn't reduce it.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Best Practices for Improving Visualforce Performance / View State

questions.q: Both extension classes and the standard controller define a `public PageReference save()` method. Which `save()` runs when the user clicks the button?
questions.code:
<apex:page standardController="Account" extensions="AuditExt,DiscountExt">
  <apex:form>
    <apex:commandButton value="Save" action="{!save}"/>
  </apex:form>
</apex:page>
options: The standard controller's `save()`
`DiscountExt.save()`, because the last extension wins
All three run in order
`AuditExt.save()`, because the leftmost extension takes precedence
questions.explain: When several extensions define the same method, the **leftmost** one wins. `AuditExt` is first, so its `save()` runs. It also overrides the standard controller's `save()`.
wrong: Extensions override standard controller methods with the same name.
Precedence runs left to right, so the last one doesn't win.
Only one method runs, never all three.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Building a Controller Extension

questions.q: A Visualforce call center page must refresh its "open calls" panel automatically every 15 seconds without reloading the whole page. Which component should be used?
options: `apex:actionPoller` with `interval="15"` and `rerender` set to the panel Id
`apex:actionStatus`
`apex:actionRegion`
`apex:outputLink`
questions.explain: To refresh a panel on a timer, use the timer tag. `apex:actionPoller` calls an action every `interval` seconds and can rerender just that panel.
wrong: `actionStatus` only shows the status of an AJAX request.
`actionRegion` limits which part of the form is processed; it has no timer.
`outputLink` is just a plain link.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: apex:actionPoller

questions.q: Clicking Show sets `showDetails` to true, but the details panel never appears. What is the fix?
questions.code:
<apex:commandButton value="Show" action="{!toggle}" rerender="details"/>
<apex:outputPanel id="details" rendered="{!showDetails}">
  ...
</apex:outputPanel>
options: Add `immediate="true"` to the `commandButton`
Wrap the panel in an always-rendered `apex:outputPanel` with an Id, and rerender that
Mark `showDetails` as `transient`
Replace `rerender` with `reRender="{!showDetails}"` so the panel redraws whenever the flag changes
questions.explain: You can only redraw something that's already on the page. A panel with `rendered="false"` at load leaves nothing to replace. Wrap it in an always-drawn `outputPanel` and rerender the wrapper.
wrong: `immediate` skips validation; it doesn't fix the missing page element.
A transient variable would lose its value between requests.
`rerender` takes component Ids, not a Boolean.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Using AJAX / Partial Page Updates

questions.q: A Visualforce page with a large view state needs a fast type-ahead search. Each keystroke must send the search text to Apex and get matching records back in a JavaScript callback. Which approach is best?
options: `apex:actionSupport` on the input, with `rerender` on the results table
`apex:actionFunction` called on every keystroke
A `static` `@RemoteAction` method called with `Visualforce.remoting.Manager.invokeAction`
`apex:actionPoller` every second
questions.explain: For fast, frequent calls on a heavy page, skip the view state. JavaScript remoting sends no view state, runs async, and hands data straight to a JS callback. It's the lightest option.
wrong: Each request sends the large view state, which is slow.
